title: FAQ
section: How much time should I spend on RSiP?
text:
How much time should I spend on RSiP?                         The Research Skills in Psychology course in this program is worth 5 ECTS. This is equivalent to 140 hours of work for each student. It is very likely that you will need less time, since multiple students will be working on the same parts. At the same time, it is also likely that you will have weeks where you are spending less time on the project (e.g., during exam weeks, while waiting for feedback, etc.) and weeks where you are spending more time (e.g., right before a deadline). Therefore, it is important to be mindful of everyone's schedule in order to successfully complete this project.                                       I heard from my friends that they are doing something differently. Why are we not expected to do it the same way?                                 A RSiP project, and generally any scientific project, does not have one way of being done. There are many valid, acceptable, and evidence-supported approaches that can be taken depending on both needs of the project and the supervisor's preferred way of working. If you believe something can be done better, I am very happy to learn about your idea and potentially integrate it!                                What if my group wants to change a deadline?                   Some deadlines in the course are strict and unchangeable, since they are given by the course coordinator and not the supervisor. The other deadlines are dependent on agreement with supervisor. If your group collectively agrees on moving a date of a deadline, you can contact me with proposed alternatives. However, moving a deadline likely means we have to move a meeting, since they are structured around the completed work. 
    For that reason, please also include at least two separate dates and a time span of 3 hours per date (e.g., February 1 between 12:00 and 15:00) on which the group is available to have the meeting.

title: FAQ
text:
Content
                        How many references should we include in the report?                                 This is a very common question, and it is one that (unfortunately for you) does not have an answer. I have read theses that included anywhere from 25 to 100+. The number of references does not provide any indication for the quality of the written work. However, lack of references can lead to plagiarism, unsupported claims, weak arguments, and worse final evaluation. Therefore, always remember to provide references for all of the claims/arguments you make, even if it is something you consider general knowledge.

title: FAQ
text:
Special circumstances
                        What if a group member is not  contributing,
communicating, and/or adhering to our agreements?                     As you know, RSiP is a group project and you are (mostly) being graded as a group. Grading is based on the assumption that the group worked together, showcasing a joint effort of 4-6 people. 
If a member is clearly not contributing, it is important to  contact me  as soon as possible. The sooner you do so, the sooner the problem will be solved.
The problems will be solved according to the step-by-step plan outlined in the syllabus. In short, if you notice someone is not contributing, the first order of business is to hold a group discussion with the member. After that, you should inform me about the situation and agreements you reached.

If the situation persists, we will organize a meeting in which I will be present to discuss this further and agree on next steps. Finally, if no improvement is noticed after that, the student may be excluded from the course.

title: Research Skills in Psychology: A Handbook
Research Skills in Psychology: A Handbook
text:
Introduction
Welcome! On this website, you will be able to find all materials needed for the successful completion of the Research Skills in Psychology (RSiP) course.
This website was created by me, your supervisor - Lucija Sorić. It exists to simplify our workflows and offer a centralized platform that is easy to find (it is just one link!) and easy to share (still just one link!).
Some parts of this website are static, and unlikely to undergo major change. For example, contact details will always remain the same.
Other aspects, such as research materials, instructions, meeting summaries, and others, will be updated at the appropriate time. The Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) section will be updated regularly, as more questions come in. This way, I am trying to ensure all of you can benefit from shared information, even if you were not the one to ask it.
Thanks for reading and looking forward to working with you!

What to include in RSiP-related emails?
It is important to include as much detail as possible so that the back-and-forth exchange is limited and you get an adequate response as soon as possible.
For example, if your question is related to certain sections, for each section you can include:

Introduction: relevant context, references, what you already have, what you need…
Methods: what you have done so far, what options you considered…
Results: what you want to achieve, what you did to get there, what you would like me to do to help you…
Discussion: relevant context, references, arguments you are unsure about…

This list is not exhaustive, and can vary per needs. However, in all project-related exchanges make sure to highlight what you have tried so far and what you need help with. If you have not tried anything yet, it is likely my response would not be sufficient to solve your problem.


Reply frequency
The teaching time allocated to me is limited. This means that apart from teaching RSIP, I have additional responsibilities with their own deadlines. Therefore, you can expect to receive a reply any time within 5 working days*. I will likely reply a lot sooner, but keep this in mind when planning your work. For example, if you only start working on a section a few days before the deadline and get stuck, it is possible you will not be able to get help on time.
* If it has been longer than this, and I am not on holiday, please send me a reminder. However, sending reminders too early is prohibited and could affect your final grade (namely, the work attitude section in the rubric).

title: 1  Proposal
text:
Why do we need a research proposal?
A research proposal is one of the most important parts of a research project. It formulates a theoretical background and a specific plan you aim to follow.
Every project, academic or not, needs a plan. A research proposal is essentially a formalized, written plan of your future steps.
When doing academic research, there are often many roads you can take - or many ways a project can go. This is true for any project, too. For example, if you want to paint a wall, you can choose between many colors! However, some of these options are more logical than others. Maybe you do not like some of the colors, maybe some colors are not available, maybe some colors clash with the furniture you own… In order to move forward with your project you have to make some decisions (i.e., choose a color), and you have to be able to explain this decision (at least to yourself).
A research proposal helps you think ahead since it asks you to make certain decisions prior to starting. By completing this step, you will save your future self a lot of time.

title: 1  Proposal
section: How do we write a research proposal in a group?
text:
How do we write a research proposal in a group?

Read the literature previously shared with you. You can read all of it, or you can split up the work with your group members.
Find a set of variables you are genuinely interested in exploring and share them with your group.
Think about the measures and analyses you can use to research these variables. Refer to the planned questionnaires and scales*. Share this with your group.
* Do not plan to mix questionnaires into one variable, and do not split them up unless you have a good reason (or a published paper provided a good argument for it).
Together with your group, decide which variables to go with. Try to assess if your statistical knowledge can properly research these variables.
Formulate a research question and hypotheses with this set of variables.
Write all the plans up, together with all other parts of the proposal.

In practice, it takes a few tries to complete step 4. It is likely that you will have to go through the steps 2 and 3 multiple times, each time reading more literature in order to improve your research question. This is normal and part of the process.

title: 1  Proposal
section: What do we include in a research proposal?
text:
What do we include in a research proposal?
Please only follow the below guidelines when writing your proposal. The word count is an estimate, and you are welcome to go a bit over if needed. However, try to be as concise as possible while not losing important information.
There is no minimum or maximum amount of citations you should include. However, it is unlikely for the proposal to be written according to the guidelines without a substantial amount of citations.

Scientific background (~200 words)
Briefly describe the current state of the literature that led to your project idea. Provide definitions/descriptions of relevant concepts. Give more attention to a few key studies that directly address your research question.


Objectives & implications (~150 words)
Clearly describe the aims of your project. Describe how your research complements the current literature, or how it fits a gap. Argue why this is important to do. You can argue for real-life relevance, too, not just for scientific benefit. These should all follow from the previously described background. You can include your research question here.


What even is a research question?


It is generally defined as the “question” that your project aims to solve. This definition, while correct, probably does not help you much in constructing your own research question. Below I will share tips on how to think about research questions.
What a research question IS?

A statement that
Is short and clear and that
Can be used to quickly and accurately tell the reader what the goal of your work is

What a research question is NOT?

A question
A research question can be in any form. In scientific literature, a research question is rarely written out in the form of a question.
Some examples:

We aimed to explore whether a leads to b.
Our research investigates how x changes y when…
This work answers the following question: How does…?

A value judgment
A research question cannot be biased. It has to be as neutral as possible. Therefore, you can never research why something is good or bad.
General
A research question only guides a scientific project, and is only informative of the work you will be doing within it. Therefore, it does not reflect potential implications and it should not promise something your project will not be solving.





Hypotheses (as many words as needed)
Formulate clear, specific hypotheses based on your research question. You can have multiple hypotheses, but you can also have just one - it is fully dependent on your question. For each hypothesis, state an expectation, explain how this expectation follows from previous literature.


How do I write a good hypothesis?


You start with a hook of sorts followed by a general topic introduction. This topic introduction is put into context through a literature review where you show what we know now, what we could know, and why this matters. Finally, you show how your work helps us know more.
An expectation (or a hypothesis) needs to be specific - it is not enough to state you expect something to be different.
Example of a bad expectation:

I hypothesize I will/expect to find a difference in trust in science between the two groups.

Example of a good expectation:

I hypothesize I will/expect to find lower scores (this specifies the difference) on questionnaires measuring beliefs in science (this specifies the variable and the measure) in men compared to women (this specifies the direction of difference).*

* This would be even better if you state the exact difference you expect. E.g., you expect to find scores that are at least 5 points lower. Remember: be as specific as possible.




Methods (~400 words)
For each section, provide a clear description and motivation for the choice made.

Design
Briefly address the study design (e.g., cross-sectional, longitudinal). State what type of measures will be used (e.g., self-reports) and where data collection will take place (e.g., online).


Participants
Indicate the expected characteristics of the sample, namely mention the sample size and the population you want to sample. The population will most likely be undergraduate students at Tilburg University. However, in case of availability, the population could focus on other groups (e.g., adults, specific genders, etc.). This is to be determined.


Measures
Describe each variable of your study, how it is measured, and what the expected output of the measure will be (e.g., a singular number, a score, a category). For questionnaires, include the name of the questionnaires, scale values (e.g., Likert scale from 1 to 5, with 1 =… , 2 = …), provide examples of questions. Always cite the original creator of the questionnaire. Provide psychometric data (i.e., reliability metrics such as Cronbach’s alpha) of questionnaires if available in previous work.


Statistical analysis

Program
Indicate the program and the version of the program you plan to use for your analyses. You can use any program you want, including SPSS and R. It is likely that all of you will use SPSS, but I can also guide you through analyses in other software.


Power
Execute and report a power analysis. This is an important step at this stage. You can use G*Power software. Provide a screenshot of the output you got.


Analysis
Indicate which statistical tests you will use, and describe the outcomes that would confirm or reject your hypothesis. The statistical test you choose has to be able to answer your hypothesis. If you are in doubt, reach out - or change your research question.
It is possible your research question may need a statistical method you are not yet familiar with. In that case you have to change your research question. Be mindful of the questions that can be answered with your current statistical knowledge. It is always better to have correct but simple analyses instead of incorrect but complicated ones.

title: 1  Proposal
section: How do we format the proposal?
text:
How do we format the proposal?
Use the standard formatting: APA-style, Times New Roman, 12-point font, line spacing 2.0. Include page numbers.

title: 1  Proposal
section: How do we split up the work?
text:
How do we split up the work?
This is entirely up to you. However, it is important to consider the implications of assigning the entire task to a sub-group or an individual. Below I note some things you could consider.

The first three sections of a proposal will serve as a basis for your introduction section. The introduction should be built on the ideas included here. Some parts can also be repeated word-for-word, and some have to be repeated (e.g., the hypotheses).
The methods section of the proposal will closely mirror your general methods section. The project’s methods section will be very similar to this one.
What is written in a proposal should not be changed much in the future. Meaning, if there are no large issues with your proposal, your future tasks will fully depend on what you included in there. This means that it would be optimal for the entire group to participate in (at least) the brainstorming part to ensure all of you agree on the direction you want to take.
In the next group meeting, you will be presenting this proposal. This is because a presentation is an integral, graded part of this course, and presentation skills require a lot of practice. I would suggest having 1-2 members present, and ideally these will not be the members that wrote the proposal. All of you should be able to talk about the ideas behind it.

title: Topic
text:
Project Description
Public Valuation of Publicly Funded Research
In 2025, the Dutch Research Council (NWO), spent 1.3 billion euros on research funding (NWO, 2026). In the same year, the European Research Council (ERC), the main public body for research funding in Europe, made more than 2.7 billion euros available for research grants (European Research Council, 2024). National and regional research councils receive their budget primarily from national governments, funded in turn by taxation on private citizens and businesses. While research suggests that public funding of science tends to align with what the public uses and benefits from at the aggregate level (Yin et al., 2022), it remains unclear whether individual citizens themselves notice this, too.
In this project, you will explore how the public values the projects it pays for, and what factors shape these judgments. Together with other students, you will collect experimental and self-report data via an online task and select a subset of variables to test your hypothesis.
